div.head: THE FIRST ACT

p.hi: A rocky cavern in a wood, in which stands a naturally formed smith's forge, with big bellows. Mime sits in front of the anvil, busily hammering at a sword.

div.p: [Who has been hammering with a small hammer, stops working.

lg.l: Can snap in two at one stroke,
As if the thing were a toy!

div.p: [Mime throws the sword on the anvil ill-humouredly, and with his arms akimbo gazes thoughtfully on the ground.

lg.l: Could I but forge the weapon,
Shame and toil would win their reward!

div.p: [He sinks further back his head bowed in thought.

lg.l: With his gruesome and grisly bulk
The only sword for the deed
Were Nothung, if it were swung

div.p: [He lays the sword in position again, and goes on hammering in deep dejection.

lg.l: He snaps in two what I make,
And scolds if I cease from work.

div.p: [In rough forester's dress, with a silver horn hung by a chain, bursts in boisterously from the wood. He is leading a big bear by a rope of bast, and urges him towards Mime in wanton fun.
[Mime drops the sword in terror, and takes refuge behind the forge; while Siegfried, shouting with laughter, keeps driving the bear after him.
Mime at the anvil. See p. 2
Then thou art safe for to-day!
[He lets the bear loose and strikes him on the back with the rope.
[The bear runs back into the wood.
MIME [Comes trembling from behind the forge.

lg.l: But why thus bring the beasts

div.p: [Sits down to recover from his laughter.

lg.l: Than the one who sits at home,
I blew my horn in the wood,
What I asked with the note
From the covert came a bear
Who listened to me with growls,
And I liked him better than thee,
Though better friends I shall find.
To ask thee, rogue, for the weapon.

div.p: [He jumps up and goes towards the anvil.
[Takes up the sword to hand it to Siegfried.

lg.l: In its sharpness thou wilt rejoice.

div.p: [He holds the sword anxiously in his hand; Siegfried snatches it from him.

lg.l: What matters an edge keen sharpened,
Unless hard and true the steel?

div.p: [He strikes it on the anvil, so that the splinters fly about. Mime shrinks back in terror.

lg.l: I would break him in bits
The doting fool of a gnome!—
And end the annoyance at once!

div.p: [Siegfried throws himself on to a stone seat in a rage. Mime all the time has been cautiously keeping out of his way.

lg.l: If what for him I forge
Is not perfect on the spot,
The good things I have made!
Thou shouldst be glad to obey him

div.p: [Siegfried turns his back on Mime in a bad temper, and sits with his face to the wall.
Thou dost not like to be told that!
[He stands perplexed, then goes to the hearth in the kitchen.

lg.l: But thou wouldst fain be fed.
Wilt eat the meat I have roasted,
Or wouldst thou prefer the broth?

div.p: [He brings food to Siegfried, who, without turning round, knocks both bowl and meat out of his hand.
MIME [In a wailing voice, as if hurt.
Mime and the infant Siegfried. See p. 8.
[Has turned round again and has quietly watched Mime's face, while the latter, meeting the look, tries timidly to hide his own.

lg.l: Thou hast taught me much, Mime,
And many things I have learned;
But what thou most gladly hadst taught me
A lesson too hard has proved—
My sleep is broken and bad;
Fain were I deaf and dumb.
So much, O Mime, I love thee!
A thing I have wondered at:
And the fish in the brook,
How is it I always return?
Of thy wisdom tell me that.
My child, that ought to show thee
That Mime is dear to thy heart.
I said I could not bear thee;

div.p: [Recoils, and sits down again apart, opposite Siegfried.]

lg.l: The wildness that thou shouldst tame
Is the cause, bad boy, of that.
What we love we all long for,
And so thou dost yearn for me;
What the old bird is to the young one,
That is what careful, clever Mime
This one thing more also tell me:
That they were wives with their husbands.
And both took care of the young.
The roes in the woods, too,
The wild wolves even, and foxes.
Food was found them and brought
The mother suckled the young ones.
That I may call her mother?
Art thou then a bird or a fox?
I often have seen for myself.
I came to the limpid brook,
And the beasts and the trees
Were mirrored quite plain in the stream.
As a fish to a toad:
And when had fish toad for its father?
What in vain I pondered so long:
Yet return home in the end.
I cannot go till thou tell me
What father and mother were mine.

div.p: [Springs upon Mime, and seizes him by the throat.

lg.l: Who are my father and mother?

div.p: Siegfried sees himself in the stream. See p. 12
[After making signs with his head and hands, is released by Siegfried.

lg.l: Dost want to kill me outright!
Hands off, and the facts thou shalt hear,
As far as known to myself.
Now learn the cause of thy hatred!
And yet thou dost owe me thy life!
And this is all my reward.
And I hoped for thanks like a fool!
Who wept in the forest wild;
I helped her here to the cave,
That by the fire I might warm her.
The woman bore a child here;
I helped her as I could.

div.p: My poor mother died, then, through me?

lg.l: To my care she commended thee;
That story I often have heard.
Now say, whence came the name

div.p: Now tell me, what name was my mother's?
My mother's name thou must tell me.

lg.l: Her name I forget. Yet wait!
Sieglinde, that was the name borne
By her who gave thee to me.

div.p: Next tell me, who was my father?
Mime finds the mother of Siegfried in the forest. See p. 13
But my mother told it thee, surely.

lg.l: That I may trust thy story,

div.p: But what proof will convince thee?

lg.l: I trust thee not with my ears,
I trust thee but with mine eyes:

div.p: [After some thought takes from the place where they are concealed the two pieces of a broken sword.

lg.l: I got this from thy mother:
She said 'twas borne by thy father
In the fatal fight when he fell.
And thou shalt learn on thy limbs
How metal best should be beat!
My weapon to-day I shall win!

div.p: What wouldst thou to-day with the sword?

lg.l: And afar shall be my home;
Thy hearth is not my house,
Like the wind o'er the wood

div.p: [He looks after the retreating figure for some time in astonishment; then he goes back to the smithy and sits down behind the anvil.
[Sobbing, he sinks in despair on to a stool behind the anvil.
[Enters from the wood by the door at the back of the cave. He wears a long dark blue cloak, and, for staff, carries a spear. On his head is a round, broad-brimmed slouched hat.

lg.l: Finds my home in the forest wild?

div.p: WANDERER [Approaching very slowly step by step.

lg.l: Wanderer names me the world, smith.
Good men grudge me not welcome;
Thou wouldst not add to it, surely!
And though much thou hast found,
I need neither seeker nor finder.

div.p: [More and more anxious as he sees the Wanderer approach.

lg.l: I know enough for my needs.
So, wise one, keep on thy way.
To answer all thou shalt ask.

div.p: [Who has been staring at the Wanderer open-mouthed, now shrinks back; aside, dejectedly.

lg.l: Now how to get rid of the spy?
The questions asked must be artful.

div.p: [He summons up courage for an assumption of sternness; aloud.

lg.l: 'Tis pawned; now seek to redeem it.
Thy feet have ranged o'er the world,
Dwells in the earth's deep gorges.
Once was their ruler and lord.
To win him the world and its glory.
Of the hidden depths of earth.
Breathes on earth's back and moves there.
The race of the giants arose;
And with it gained the ring too.
Of the earth's back rude and rugged.
Deep in the shaft he cut.
All must obey, and for ever,

div.p: [He strikes the ground with the spear as if by accident, and a low growl of thunder is heard, by which Mime is violently alarmed.

lg.l: And is not my head redeemed?

div.p: [After attentively watching the Wanderer with the spear, becomes very frightened, seeks in a confused manner for his tools, and looks timidly aside.

lg.l: Forfeit my head if I failed.
The thing it would serve thee to know.
That I might rest by thy hearth.
So sharpen well, Mime, thy wits!

div.p: [Very much frightened, and after much hesitation, at last composes himself with timid submission.

lg.l: I saw here the eye of Wotan
But well were it now to be wise.
The dwarf, and redeem his head.
Tell the name of the race

div.p: And yet loves beyond all the rest.

lg.l: This question I answer with ease.
Though they are shown no grace.
The strongest shoot from the tree.
Rogue, I see thou art clever.
That the dwarf may be lord of the hoard,

div.p: [Forgetting his present situation more and more, rubs his hands joyfully.

lg.l: He who could draw it forth.
Well he fought with the sword
Till on Wotan's spear it was split.

div.p: Mime and the Wanderer. See p. 17

lg.l: Who else could so clever be!
Whose skill from the doughty splinters
I was mad to steal it!

div.p: [He throws his tools about as if he had gone crazy, and breaks out in utter despair.

lg.l: How rede aright such a riddle?

div.p: WANDERER [Has risen quietly from the hearth.

lg.l: Three things thou wert to ask me;
But what stood here at thy hand—

div.p: [Mime stares at him; he turns to go.

lg.l: I leave it forfeit to him
Who has never learned to fear.

div.p: [He turns away smiling, and disappears quickly in the wood. Mime has sunk on to the bench overwhelmed.
[Stares before him into the sunlit wood, and begins to tremble more and more violently.
[Behind the scenes, is heard breaking from the thicket.
Quick, come show me the sword.

lg.l: Where art thou? Where hidest thou?

div.p: [In a small voice, from behind the anvil.
MIME [Comes forward, greatly upset and confused.

lg.l: Where shall I turn in my need?
And forfeit to him it will fall
Who has never learned to fear.
But that lesson was one never taught thee.
And alas! the task proved hard.
Now how shall I teach thee to fear?
Something of weight I would teach thee.
What weighty thing foundest thou there?
Down there I learned how to fear,
That I might teach thee, dullard.

div.p: This fear then, what is it?

lg.l: What help in the trustiest sword,
Hadst thou not learned to fear?

div.p: [Approaching Siegfried with more and more confidence.

lg.l: That the world and its wiles
Until thou hadst learned how to fear.
Explain: this fearing, what is it?
Hast thou not felt grim horror
Hold every sense in its clutches?—
And the heart, filled with dismay,
Hast thou not yet felt that,
A stranger art thou to fear.
Beats my heart in my breast.
Ah, how glad I would feel them,
Could I but learn this delight!
How, coward, could it be taught me?
I have thought it all out.
I know of a dragon grim
Fear thou wilt learn from Fafner,
When I lead to where he lies.
Towards the end of the wood.

div.p: It lies not far from the world?
The world is quite close to the cave.

lg.l: That I may learn what this fear is,
Make haste! Forge me the sword.
In the world fain I would swing it.
Unequal my skill to the task;
By one who never felt fear.
And not seek to lie his way out.
By him shall it be forged.

div.p: [Flinging Mime's tools about, he sets himself impetuously to work.

lg.l: And now at need canst do nothing.
Had he obeyed him in all?

div.p: [He makes a contemptuous grimace at him.

lg.l: In case with the steel I melt thee.

div.p: [He has heaped a large quantity of charcoal on the hearth, and keeps blowing the fire, while he screws up the pieces of the sword in a vice and files them to shavings.
[Who has sat down a little way off, watches Siegfried at work.

lg.l: With paste I fashion no sword!
Why grind thus the steel to splinters?
Only so can splinters be patched.

div.p: [He goes on filing with great energy.

lg.l: By his own folly the fool is best served.

div.p: [Siegfried has blown the fire to a bright flame.

lg.l: The like I never yet saw!

div.p: [While Siegfried continues to file the piece of the sword impetuously, Mime seats himself a little further off.

lg.l: Forfeit it falls to the boy.

div.p: [Springing up and bending down in growing agitation.

lg.l: The dragon will never be slain;
And, if so, how gain the ring?
I must find out some way
Of subduing the boy for myself.

div.p: [Has now filed down the pieces, and puts the filings in a crucible, which he places on the fire.

lg.l: That I have pounded to pieces.

div.p: [During the following song keeps blowing the fire with the bellows.

lg.l: What blow, I wonder, broke thee.
The splinters now I am melting.
It fell, by my hand hewn down.
Now it lies heaped high on the hearth.
How clear and fair its fire!
Thy steel chopped to chaff is fused;

div.p: The forging of Nothung. See p. 34
[He pours the glowing contents of the crucible into a mould, which he holds up.
But soon my sword thou shalt be!
[During the pauses in Siegfried's song, still aside, sitting at a distance.

lg.l: So much I can clearly foresee;
How to win them both for myself!
And safe shall be my head.
For a cooling draught he will crave;
The draught I will brew for him.
Let him drink but a drop,
That he fashioned to serve him
He shall be cleared from my way,
And treasure and ring made mine.

div.p: [He springs up joyfully, fetches several vessels, shakes spices and herbs from them into a pot, and tries to put it on the hearth.
[Has plunged the mould into a pail of water. Steam and loud hissing ensue as it cools.

lg.l: That swift I may weld thee,

div.p: [He thrusts the steel into the fire, and blows the bellows violently. While doing so he watches Mime, who, from the other side of the hearth, carefully puts his pot on the fire.

lg.l: A smith is put to shame,
And learns from the lad he taught;
All the master's lore is useless now;
He serves the boy as cook.
Steel thou dost brew into broth;
And cares no longer to forge;
All the swords that he made me;
What he cooks my lips shall not touch.

div.p: [During the following he takes the mould from the fire, breaks it, and lays the glowing steel on the anvil.

lg.l: To find out what fear is
A far-off teacher shall teach me;
The warm blood cooled at thy touch!
On me who humbled thy pride.
Be as cold and hard as thou canst.

div.p: [He swings the blade, plunges it into the pail of water, and laughs aloud at the hissing.
[While Siegfried is fixing the blade in the hilt, moves about in the foreground with the bottle into which he has poured the contents of the pot. Aside.

lg.l: By guile the goal must be reached;
That ring I have won now,

div.p: [He trots briskly about with increasing satisfaction.

lg.l: To the hoard will come thronging
Hei, Mime! Great luck has been thine!
Had any one dreamed of this!

div.p: [During the pauses in Mime's song has been filing and sharpening the sword and hammering it with the small hammer. He flattens the rivets of the hilt with the last strokes, and now grasps the sword.

lg.l: Once more art thou firm in thy hilt.
No second blow thy blade shall shatter.
And for him its edge shall be keen.
Once more to life I have waked thee.

div.p: [He strikes the anvil and splits it in two from top to bottom, so that it falls asunder with a great noise. Mime, who has mounted a stool in great delight, falls in terror to a fitting position on the ground. Siegfried holds the sword exultantly on high. The curtain falls.

div.head: THE SECOND ACT

p.hi: Quite in the background the entrance to a cave. The ground rises towards a flat knoll in the middle of the stage, and slopes down again towards the back, so that only the upper part of the entrance to the cave is visible to the audience. To the left a fissured cliff is seen through the trees. It is night, the darkness being deepest at the back, where at first the eye can distinguish nothing at all.

div.p: [A storm arises in the wood on the right, and from the same quarter there shines down a bluish light.

lg.l: It runs like a horse and it shines;
Who comes there, shining in shadow?

div.p: [Enters from the wood, and stops opposite Alberich.

lg.l: In the dark who is hiding there?

div.p: [As from a sudden rent in the clouds moonlight streams forth and lights up the Wanderer's figure.
[Recognises the Wanderer and shrinks back at first in alarm, but immediately after breaks out in violent fury.

lg.l: Not deluged the earth through thy guile?
When I was bound thy captive,
To steal the ring again from me!
Of the compact made with the churls;
Thou dost not dare to despoil them:
Would crumble to dust in thy hand.
By the steadfast runes of treaties
On thee my spear may spend its strength,
So keen I keep it for war.
And yet full of fear is thy heart!
Belong as before to the Niblung?—
That gnaws thee with ceaseless torment.
For once I have got it
And rule, lord of the world!
But to me all is plain.
A hero begot of thy blood.
Hast thou not fostered a stripling
To pluck the fruit thou durst not
For thy brother brings here a boy
And so I say to thee,
Do as seems to thee best.

div.p: [Alberich makes a movement expressive of violent curiosity.

lg.l: The boy will hear of the ring
When Mime tells him the tale.

div.p: Wilt thou hold thy hand from the hoard?

lg.l: All my hope hangs upon heroes.

div.p: And yet it is not to be mine?

lg.l: Two Nibelungs yearn for the gold.
Then a hand, seizing, shall hold it.
Who, if warned of his death,
Gladly would give up the toy.
Come, I will wake him for thee.

div.p: [He goes towards the cave, and, standing on the rising ground in front of it, calls towards it.

lg.l: If thou wilt pay the price
With the treasure that thou guardest.

div.p: [He leans his ear towards the cave, listening.
[Has come to the Wanderer and calls into the cave.

lg.l: To try his strength against thine.

div.p:
Bold is the boy and strong;
Sharp-edged is his sword.

lg.l: Give me the ring, and so
In peace shalt thou live long!

div.p: [Laughs aloud and then turns again to Alberich.

lg.l: But call me rogue no more.
Each according to his kind must act;
I leave thee the field now;
And try thy luck with thy brother;
Thou knowest his kind perhaps better.

div.p: [He turns away, and disappears quickly in the wood. A storm arises and a bright light breaks forth; then both quickly cease.
[Looks after the Wanderer as he gallops off.

lg.l: And leaves me to care and scorn!

div.p: [He slips into the chasm at the side. The stage remains empty. Dawn.

p.hi: As the day dawns Siegfried and Mime enter. Siegfried carries his sword in a sword-belt of rope. Mime examines the place carefully. At last he looks towards the background, which remains in deep shadow, whilst the rising ground in the middle becomes, after a time, more and more brightly illuminated by the sun.

div.p: [Sits down under the lime-tree and looks about him.

lg.l: So here I shall learn what fear is?
A far way thou hast led me;
A whole night long in the woods.
The brute could swallow thee whole.
'Twere well to close up his gullet;
His fangs I will therefore avoid.
Thy body and bones would decay.

div.p:
That the poison may not consume me,
I will keep out of its reach.

lg.l: Thy limbs would be broken like glass.
That his swinging tail may not touch me,
At last thou beginnest to fear?

div.p: [Who till now has been lying indolently stretched out, sits up suddenly.

lg.l: Is that what is meant by fearing?
No fear is here to be learnt.
Thou wilt remember who brought thee,
And think of me and my love.
Out of my sight with thee;
And on the instant I go!
And rid be at length of the fool?
And rest there by the spring.
And as the sun scales the sky
Unchecked thither the brute shall go;
To the heart I stab him!
So heed well what I say:
When the fierce fight is over?

div.p: [Siegfried repeats the gesture with more violence.
Or if felled on a sudden by fear.
[Siegfried rises and drives him away with furious gestures.

lg.l: Might each the other but slay!

div.p: [He disappears in the wood on the right.
[Stretches himself at his ease under the lime-tree, and looks after Mime as he departs.

lg.l: He is no father of mine!
How merry of heart I feel!
For the loathed one has gone at last,
To be looked on by me no more.
Had Mime by chance had a son,
To see him makes me sick!

div.p: [He leans further back and looks up through the branches of the tree. Deep silence. Woodland murmurs.

lg.l: In fear and woe she bore me,
But why did she die through me?

div.p: [He sighs softly, and leans still further back. Deep silence. Louder murmuring of the wood. His attention is at last caught by the song of the birds. He listens with growing interest to one singing in the branches above him.

lg.l: Hast thou thy home in this wood?
If I could but understand him,
His sweet song might say much—
Perhaps of my mother tell me.
Of birds when they were singing;
On the reed follow him sweetly.
Perhaps I shall know what he says.

div.p: [He runs to the neighbouring spring, cuts a reed off with his sword, and quickly makes himself a pipe out of it. He listens again.

[He blows into the pipe, breaks off, and cuts it again to improve it. He resumes his blowing, shakes his head, and cuts the pipe once more. After another attempt he gets angry, presses the pipe with his hand, and tries again. He ceases playing and smiles.

lg.l: The reed is not suited at all.

div.p: [He hears the bird again and looks up to him.

lg.l: He waits, and nothing rewards him.
To a song of the woods
A merry song, listen now rather.
What comrade will come to its call.

div.p: [He takes the silver hunting-horn and blows on it. During the long-sustained notes he keeps his eyes expectantly on the bird. A movement in the background. Fafner, in the form of a monstrous lizard-like dragon, has risen from his lair in the cave. He breaks through the underwood and drags himself up to the higher ground, so that the front part of his body rests on it, while he utters a loud sound, as if yawning.
[Looks round and gazes at Fafner in astonishment. He laughs.
[At the sight of Siegfried has paused on the high ground, and remains there.

lg.l: Perchance thou couldst teach me something.
Say, wilt thou be his teacher?
With my sword I will slay thee,
Wilt thou not teach me to fear.

div.p: [He opens his jaws and shows his teeth.

lg.l: What a fine set of teeth
'Twere well if I closed up thy gullet;
Thy jaws are gaping too wide!
That without delay thou shouldst die!

div.p: [He springs towards Fafner and remains defiantly confronting him. Fafner drags himself further up the knoll and spits at Siegfried from his nostrils. Siegfried avoids the poison, springs nearer, and stands on one side. Fafner tries to reach him with his tail. Siegfried, who is nearly caught, springs over Fafner with one bound, and wounds him in the tail. Fafner roars, pulls his tail angrily away, and raises the front part of his body so that he may throw its full weight on Siegfried, thus offering his breast to the stroke. Siegfried quickly looks to see where his heart is, and thrusts his sword into it up to the hilt. Fafner raises himself still higher in his pain, and, when Siegfried has let go his sword and sprung aside, he sinks on the wound.
Lie there, envious brute! Nothung's point home has speeded!

lg.l: Who stirred up thy childish soul
Thy brain schemed not the harm
Stirred me to fight and to slay.
Who knowest not yet who thou art,
The brothers now are both fallen.
Falls, by a rosy boy slain.
He who stirred thee blind to this deed
Takes thought how to compass thy death.
That may help thee to guess.
The dead can tell no tidings.

div.p: [Fafner has rolled to the side in dying. Siegfried now draws the sword from his breast. In doing so his hand gets sprinkled with the blood; he draws it back quickly.
The hot blood burns like fire!
[Involuntarily he raises his fingers to his mouth to suck the blood from them. As he looks musingly before him his attention becomes more and more attracted by the singing of the birds.

lg.l: To hear the birds speaking to me.

div.p: [From the branches of the lime-tree above Siegfried.

lg.l: Tarnhelm, if he could but win it,
Would help him to deeds of renown;
And could he discover the ring,
It would make him the lord of the world!

div.p: "The hot blood burns like fire!" See p 58.
[Has listened holding his breath and beaming with delight.
[He turns towards the back and descends to the cave, where he at once disappears.

p.hi: Mime steals up, looking about him timidly to assure himself of Fafner's death. At the same time Alberich comes out of the cleft on the opposite side. He observes Mime, rushes on him and bars his way, as the latter turns towards the cave.

lg.l: The Rhine of gold for the ring?
Couldst aright have fashioned, thou bungler?
Forced thee to master thy craft.
'Twas reft from thy clutch by the giants.
I will gain and keep by my guile.
Who won it is now its lord.
For my pains now he shall pay;
My trouble has waited too long.
But treat me as a brother;
There will be booty for both.
Thou wouldst leave me with nothing!
Short work, dear brother, of thee!
From the cavern hither he comes.
Get him to give thee the ring now!
'Tis I, not thou, who shall win it.
Must it at last be surrendered!

div.p: [During the foregoing Siegfried, with Tarnhelm and ring, has come slowly and meditatively from the cave; he regards his booty thoughtfully, and stops on the knoll in the middle of the stage.

lg.l: How with fallen Fafner I fought,
And yet could not learn how to fear.

div.p: [He hangs the Tarnhelm on his girdle and puts the ring on his finger. Silence. His notice is involuntarily drawn to the bird again, and he listens to him with breathless attention.
The dwarfs quarrelling over the body of Fafner. See p. 59.

lg.l: Both the helm and the ring!
He were wise to be wary of
Because he has tasted the blood.

div.p: [Siegfried's mien and gestures show that he has understood the bird's song. He sees Mime approaching, and remains without moving, leaning on his sword, observant and self-contained, in his place on the knoll till the close of the following scene.
[Steals forward, and observes Siegfried from the foreground.

lg.l: The insolent boy I may fool.

div.p: [He goes nearer to Siegfried and welcomes him with flattering gestures.

lg.l: Hast thou been taught how to fear?

div.p: A teacher still is to find.

lg.l: A fell and fierce monster was he.
Though grim and spiteful the brute,
The one who bade me slay
I hate far more than the slain.
Soon thine eyelids will be sealed.
For me is to win the booty.
Methinks that task will not tax me;
Thou wert always easy to fool.

div.p: To me thou art plotting harm, then?

lg.l: Thee and all that are like thee.
That I reared thee with care:
The gold hid in Fafner's cave
I worked for as my reward.

div.p: [As if he were promising him something nice.
[As if he were ready to lay down his life for him.
I have no choice but to slay thee!

lg.l: But must I lose my life for thy pleasure?
While thy blade thou didst melt
And mine the hoard and Tarnhelm too.
And all it has won me—
Why wilt mistake so my words!
Take this: the drink will refresh thee
As my drinks oft have done.
The draughts I brought thou hast swallowed.
Say, how has this one been brewed?

div.p: [Jesting merrily, as if describing to him a pleasant state of intoxication which the liquor is to bring about.

lg.l: Soon shall thy senses be sunk;
None to watch or ward them,
To take the booty and hide it;
Then I shall have both rest and the ring!

div.p: Thou wouldst, then, slay me when sleeping?
Do what, child? Did I say that?
[He takes pains to assume the utmost tenderness. Carefully and distinctly.
[With the appearance of heartfelt solicitude for Siegfried's health.

lg.l: I should never dare to pause
Till from my path I thrust thee:
How else could I come by the booty,

div.p: [He pours the liquid into the drinking-horn, and offers it to Siegfried with pressing gestures.

lg.l: Drink the draught and be choked,

div.p: [As if seized by violent loathing, he gives Mime a sharp stroke with his sword. Instantly Mime falls dead to the ground. Alberich's voice in mocking laughter from the cleft.
[Looking at Mime on the ground, quietly hangs his sword again on his belt.

lg.l: 'Twas for this that I forged him.

div.p: [He picks up Mime's body, carries it to the knoll, and throws it into the cave.

lg.l: Now let it belong to its master!

div.p: [With a great effort he pushes the body of the dragon in front of the entrance to the cave, which it completely stops up.

lg.l: Thou shalt guard the glittering gold:
So both at last shall rest in peace.

div.p: [He looks down thoughtfully into the cave for a time, and then turns slowly to the front of the stage as if tired. He passes his hand over his brow.

lg.l: My hand burns on my head.
High stands the sun in heaven;
Through a cloudless sky on my crown.
Pleasant shadows will cool me under the linden.

div.p: [He stretches himself out under the lime-tree, and again looks up through the boughs.

lg.l: I could once more hear thee singing!
On a branch I see thee
At last I was forced to slay him.

div.p: [He looks sorrowfully up at the branches.

lg.l: Wilt thou choose for me the right one?
And yet no one has come!
So wise thy counsel has been.

div.p: Now sing! I hearken to thy song.

lg.l: She sleeps where rugged rocks soar;
Ringed is her chamber by fire.
Forth from the wood to the fell!
Say, shall I break through the fire?
Dear bird, that dullard am I!
To find out what fear was from Fafner.
Now from Brünnhild' to learn it.
What path soonest leads to the fell?

div.p: [The bird flutters up, circles over Siegfried, and flies hesitatingly before him.

lg.l: The bird to my goal will guide me.

div.p: [He runs after the bird, who for a time flies uncertainly hither and thither to tease him; at last he follows him, when, taking a definite direction towards the back, the bird flies away.

div.head: THE THIRD ACT

p.hi: A wild spot at the foot of a rocky mountain which rises precipitously at the back on the left. Night, storm, lightning and violent thunder. The latter ceases shortly, but the lightning continues to flash from the clouds for some time. The Wanderer enters and walks resolutely towards a cavernous opening in a rock in the foreground, and takes up his position there, leaning on his spear, while he calls the following towards the entrance to the cave.

div.p: [A dim bluish light begins to dawn in the cavern. In this light Erda, during the following, rises very gradually from below. She appears to be covered with hoar-frost, which glitters on her hair and garments.

lg.l: Who wakes me from my sleep?
That I might ask of thee counsel,
I have called thee from sleep.
And deftly weave what I know.
The Norns thou shouldst have questioned.
How a wheel on the roll can be stayed.
My mind grows through men's deeds.
The Wala's self to his will.
When, sorely urged, himself he controlled.
When the fight was at fiercest,
He pressed slumber into her eyes,
On the flame-girt rock she sleeps.
That she may love and wed with a man.
Small hope of answer from her.
Does the deed he urged to
Let me down to the dark,
I will not let thee descend,
For a potent magic I wield.
My mind was fettered by fear.
How a God may conquer his care.
Why art thou come, wild and wayward,
What, with myself at war, in anguish,
Mad with disgust I decreed once
The world to the Nibelung's hate,
But now to the valiant Wälsung
For no fear does he know.
A deed to redeem the world.

div.p: [Erda, whose eyes are already closed, and who has gradually been sinking deeper, disappears entirely. The cavern has become quite dark again.

p.hi: Dawn lights up the stage; the storm has ceased. The Wanderer has gone close to the cave, and leans with his back against it, facing the wings.

div.p: [He remains where he is without changing his position. Siegfried's wood-bird flutters towards the foreground. Suddenly the bird stops in his direct flight, flutters to and fro in alarm, and disappears quickly towards the back.

lg.l: My bird has vanished from sight!
Blithely he showed me the way,
And then forsook me and fled!
The path I followed so far
That by flaming fire is surrounded:
Taught thee to yearn for the woman?
That fell before me at Neidhöhl'—
When the sense of the singer grew plain.
Who was it urged thee on
And slay this dragon so dread?
What fear is fain he had taught me.
For he threatened me with his jaws.
That it slew the daunting foe?
Swordless else I should have been still.
From which the sword was welded strong?
That the splintered steel was useless
Were not the sword forged anew.
Keep me no longer here talking.
More need to show me due honour.
Him I at last swept aside.

div.p: That thou like Mime shalt fare.
[He goes still nearer to the Wanderer.

lg.l: And why hangs it so over thy face?
That is the way I wear it
When against the wind I go.
But an eye beneath it is wanting.
The other thou shalt lose also!
Thou lookest now on the other
That still is left me for sight.

div.p: [Who has been listening thoughtfully, now bursts involuntarily into hearty laughter.

lg.l: Thy foolish talk sets me laughing!
But come, this nonsense must finish.
At once show me my way;
Then proceed thou too on thine own;
So speak, or off thou shalt pack!
Thy scoffs I had been spared!
It would ruin both thee and me.
Was guiding when he flew off.

div.p: [Breaking out in anger and assuming a commanding attitude.

lg.l: In fear of its life it fled.
Dire his plight were he caught!

div.p: [Amazed, falls hack and assumes a defiant attitude.

lg.l: That wilt not let me pass?
Holds the maiden fettered by sleep.

div.p: [He points with his spear towards the rocky heights.
[A flickering glow, increasing in brightness, appears on the summit of the rock.

lg.l: For where the fire is burning,

div.p: [He advances; the Wanderer bars his way.

lg.l: Hast thou no fear of the fire,
Then barred by my spear be thy path!
My sword will hew it in twain!

div.p: [With one stroke he hews the Wanderer's spear in two pieces. Lightning flashes from the spear up towards the rocks, where the light, until now dim, begins to flame brighter and brighter. A violent thunder-clap, which quickly dies away, accompanies the stroke.
[Quietly picking up the pieces of the spear which have fallen at his feet.
Fare on! I cannot prevent thee!
[The growing brightness of the clouds of fire, which keep sinking down lower and lower, attracts Siegfried's eye.

lg.l: Through fire I will win to the bride!
To summon a comrade I call!

div.p: [He sets his horn to his lips and plunges into the fiery billows, which, flowing down from the heights, now spread over the foreground. Siegfried, who is soon lost to view, seems, from the sound of his horn, to be ascending the mountain. The flames begin to fade, and change gradually into a dissolving cloud lit by the glow of dawn.

p.hi: The thin cloud has resolved itself into a fine rose-coloured veil of mist, which so divides that the upper part rises and disappears, disclosing the bright blue sky of day; whilst on the edge of the rocky height, now becoming visible (exactly the same scene as in the third Act of "The Valkyrie"), a veil of mist reddened by the dawn remains hanging, which suggests the magic fire still flaming below. The arrangement of the scene is exactly the same as at the end of "The Valkyrie." In the foreground, under a wide-spreading fir-tree, lies Brünnhilde in full shining armour, her helmet on her head, and her long shield covering her, in deep sleep.

div.p: [Coming from the back, reaches the rocky edge of the summit, and at first shows only the upper part of his body. He looks round him for a longtime in amaze. Softly.
[He climbs to the summit, and, standing on a rock at the edge of the precipice at the back, gazes at the scene in astonishment. He looks into the wood at the side and comes forward a little.
[Approaching slowly he stops in surprise when, still at some little distance from her, he sees Brünnhilde.

lg.l: The steel, how it gleams and glints!

div.p: [He lifts up the shield and sees Brünnhilde's form; her face, however, is for the most part hidden by her helmet.

lg.l: The sight stirs thoughts sweet and strange!

div.p: [He loosens the helmet carefully and removes it from the head of the sleeper. Long curling hair breaks forth. Tenderly.

lg.l: Ought I to loosen the breastplate?

div.p: [He draws his sword and gently and carefully cuts through the rings on both sides of the breastplate; he then lifts this off along with the greaves, so that Brünnhilde now lies before him in a soft woman's robe. He draws back startled and amazed.
[He stares at the sleeper, greatly excited.

lg.l: I reel, my heart faints and fails!
I reel, my heart faints and fails!"

div.p: [He sinks as if fainting on to Brünnhilde's bosom; then he starts up sighing.

lg.l: What if her gaze strike me blind!
Has taught him what fear is at last!

div.p: [As he approaches the sleeping figure again he is overcome by tenderer emotions at the light. He bends down lower; sweetly.

lg.l: Of lips I will suck, then,

div.p: [He sinks, as if dying, on to the sleeping figure, and, closing his eyes, fastens his lips on Brünnhilde's. Brünnhilde opens her eyes. Siegfried starts up, and remains standing before her.
[Rises slowly to a sitting posture. Raising her arms, she greets the earth and sky with solemn gestures on her return to consciousness.
[Awed and entranced by her look and her voice, stands as if spellbound.

lg.l: Hail, O Earth, in thy glory!
So that I see those eyes
Beam on me, blest among men!
No eye dared see me but thine;
To thee alone might I wake!

div.p: [Both remain full of beaming ecstasy, lost in mutual contemplation.

lg.l: O joy of the world, couldst know
So long loved wert thou, Siegfried!
My mother did not die, then?
Did the dear one but sleep?

div.p: [Smiles and stretches her hand out kindly towards him.

lg.l: Nevermore thy mother will greet thee!
If I be blest with thy love.
Divined the thought hid by Wotan:
Was love of thee, nothing but that!
But dark the meaning to me.
But what thou sayest I strive
Thou hast taught me at last;

div.p: [He remains in great excitement with his yearning gaze fixed on her.
[Turns her head gently aside and looks towards the wood.

lg.l: He too has by Siegfried been waked.
For the pasture sweet that I look on!

div.p: [Points to her armour, which she now perceives.

lg.l: It shields, it hides me no more!
I came without shield or helm!
From the form of the maiden
Nor shelter nor shield is left
To the weak and sorrowful maid!
Are burning now in my breast!

div.p: [Springs up, resists him with the utmost strength of terror, and flies to the other side of the stage.

lg.l: No God's touch have I known!
He has broken breastplate and helm;
Now I am Brünnhild' no more.
Awake, be a woman to me!
Its light from thy love of me?

div.p: [She hides her eyes with her hands in violent terror.
[Gently removing her hands from her eyes.

lg.l: Rise from the dark and behold:
Bright as the sun is the day.
Bright as the sun shines the day!
And always to make thee blest!
Bring me not under thy yoke,
Undo not the loved one so dear!
Thy face would not be there,
O bring not thine own to naught!
My yearning lost in the flood!
Be mine! Be mine! Be mine!
And wilt be, be thou it now!
The fear and the fever would vanish
By the blaze of my eyes
As my blood like a torrent
As the blood swift-surging is kindled,
As our eyes devour one another,
As our arms cling close in their rapture,

div.p: [With the last words he has involuntarily let Brünnhilde go.
[While Brünnhilde repeats the foregoing, beginning at "Farewell Walhall's Radiant world."
Brünnhilde throws herself into Siegfried's arms. See p. 99.
[Brünnhilde throws herself into Siegfried's arms. The curtain falls.

row.cell:
THE HALL OF GUNTHER'S DWELLING ON THE RHINE.
THE VALKYRIES' ROCK
A WOODED REGION ON THE RHINE. GUNTHER'S HALL

div.head: PRELUDE

p.hi: The curtain rises slowly. The scene is the same as at the close of the second day, on the Valkyries' rock; night. In the background, from below, firelight shines. The three Norns, tall women in long, dark, veil-like drapery. The first (eldest) lies in the foreground, to the right, under the spreading pine-tree; the second (younger) is stretched on a shelving rock in front of the cave; the third (youngest) fits in the centre at the back on a rock near the peak. Motionless, gloomy silence.

lg.l: Glows in flame around the rock.
Why spin we not, singing the while?
Where for our spinning and singing

div.p: [While she loosens a golden rope from herself and ties one end of it to a branch of the pine-tree.

lg.l: I sing and wind the rope
Badly or well, as may be.
The boughs of a sacred wood.
Came to drink at the well;
He paid with the loss of an eye.
And shaped the shaft of a spear.
As time rolled on the wood
Wasted and died of the wound;
Here on the pine-tree my rope.

div.p: [Winds the rope thrown to her round a projecting rock at the entrance of the cave.

lg.l: Which wielding, he swayed the world.
In fight then splintered the spear,
With its treaties cleaving in twain.
Both the stem and boughs sere and barren.
Sealed was the fountain that flowed.
Of the rock I wind the rope:

div.p: [Catching the rope and throwing the end behind her.

lg.l: With the Gods and the holy
Shall the fair hall be consumed.
And then shall the high Gods' downfall
Spin and sing, O my sister.

div.p: [She throws the rope to the second Norn and the second throws it to the first, who loosens the rope from the bough and ties it on to another.

lg.l: Dost thou know how he fared?

div.p: [Winding the rope which has been thrown to her round the rock again.

lg.l: The solemn runes on the shaft.
Canst thou tell us the end?
The blazing one deep in the breast;
Hewn logs heaped ready for burning.

div.p: [She throws the rope back; the second Norn winds it up and throws it again to the first.

lg.l: The strands are twisted and loose.

div.p: [With laborious haste winds the rope round the jagged rock at the mouth of the cave.
[Hastily catching the rope which is thrown to her.

lg.l: Its end can reach to the north!

div.p: [She pulls hard at the rope, which breaks.
[They take the pieces of broken rope and bind their bodies together with them.
[They vanish. The dawn grows brighter; the firelight from the valley gradually fades. Sunrise; then broad daylight.

p.hi: Siegfried and Brünnhilde enter from the cave. He is fully armed; she leads her horse by the bridle.

lg.l: The things the Gods taught me
Thy gifts than I can guard!
O chide not if thy teaching
To that lore I hold fast;
And one lesson I have learned—
If thou wouldst truly love me,
And of thy deeds of daring!
That fearless thou didst fare through
When around the rock it burned—
Think too of the shield-hidden maid
Thou didst find there lapped in slumber.
And whose helmet hard thou didst break—
Will deeply burn then for aye!
Must I leave thee, O love,
In thy holy fortress of fire,

div.p: [He has taken Alberich's ring from his finger, and holds it out to Brünnhilde.

lg.l: This ring of mine I give thee;
Let it pay for thy runes.
By my hand was the dragon grim,
Who long had guarded it, slain;
Keep thou the gold and its might
As token true of my love!

div.p: [Putting on the ring in rapturous delight.

lg.l: I covet it more than all else!
For the ring take Grane, my horse.
But if thou lead the way,
Then every deed that I dare
Will be achieved through thy virtue
All my battles thou wilt choose,
And my victories will be thine.

div.p: Siegfried leaves Brünnhilde in search of adventure. See p. 111.
O were but Brünnhilde thy soul too!
Through her my courage burns high.
Then wert thou Siegfried and Brünnhild'.
Where I am, there thy abode is.
Then a waste is my hall of rock?

[Siegfried leads the horse quickly to the edge of the sloping rock, Brünnhilde following him. Siegfried disappears with the horse down behind the projecting rock, so that he is no longer visible to the audience. Brünnhilde is thus suddenly left standing alone on the edge of the slope, and gazes down into the valley after Siegfried. Her gestures show that Siegfried has vanished from her sight. Siegfried's horn is heard from below. Brünnhilde listens, and steps further out on the slope. She catches sight of Siegfried in the valley again, and waves to him joyfully. Her happy smiles seem to reflect the air of the merrily departing hero.

div.head: THE FIRST ACT

p.hi: The hall of the Gibichungs on the Rhine. This is quite open at the back. An open shore stretching to the river occupies the background. Rocky heights enclose the shore. Gunther and Gutrune on a throne at one side, before which stands a table with drinking-vessels on it. In front of this Hagen is seated.

lg.l: Is my fame on the Rhine
To me by Grimhild' our mother.
That the Gibichung has not yet won.
Whom wouldst thou have me woo,
Her chamber is circled by fire;
And he who would Brünnhild' woo
Must break through the daunting flame.

div.p: Suffices my strength for the task?
For one stronger still it is decreed.

lg.l: Had as their offspring this child.
In the woods he grew and waxed strong.
Tell me what deed of high valour
Made this hero the first in renown.
The fame of the hero dawned.
They say that a priceless treasure
The Niblungs had in their hoard.
The man who could use its spell
Were lord of the world evermore.

div.p: And Siegfried won it in fight?
He has the Niblungs in thrall.
And Brünnhild' no other can win?
To no other will the flames yield.
[He walks to and fro much agitated.
[Without leaving his seat causes Gunther to pull up as he approaches him, by a gesture of mysterious import.

lg.l: Were she by Siegfried brought home?
But how could I force this man
To woo the bride for me?
Thy simple prayer would force him,
What arts have I to bind him?
Has long ere this by the fairest

div.p: What of the drink in the chest?

lg.l: In me who won it have more faith.
To thee in love it will bind
Him whom thy heart most desires.

div.p: [Gunther has come to the table again, and, leaning against it, pays close attention.

lg.l: And taste of this potion of herbs,
He would straight forget he had looked
Who for brother gave us thee.

div.p: But how can he be found?
[A horn on the stage, from the background on the left, very loud but distant.

lg.l: Belike in his chase he will come,
To the Gibich's realm on the Rhine.

div.p: [A horn on the stage, nearer, but still distant. Both listen.
A horn from the Rhine I hear.
[Looks down the river and calls towards the back.

lg.l: A man and horse on board a boat!
His horn how gaily he winds!

div.p: [A horn on the stage sounds nearer. Gunther stops half-way listening.
[Making a trumpet of his hands, calls towards the river.
I seek the son of Gibich.
I bid thee welcome to Gunther's hall.
[Siegfried in a boat appears at the shore.
This way! Stop here and land!

p.hi: Siegfried brings his boat to the shore. Hagen makes it fast with the chain. Siegfried springs ashore with his horse. Gunther has come down and joined Hagen.

div.p: [Gutrune gazes at Siegfried from the throne in astonishment. Gunther prepares to offer him friendly greetings. All stand fixed in silent mutual contemplation.
[Leaning on his horse, remains quietly standing by the boat.
I am he thou dost seek.
[As he hands over the horse to Hagen.

[Hagen leads the horse away. While Siegfried looks thoughtfully after him, Gutrune, obeying a sign of Hagen's which Siegfried does not notice, goes to her room through a door on the left. Gunther comes into the hall with Siegfried, whom he has invited to accompany him.

lg.l: By my body I swear it!
Nor land nor folk have I to give,
As I live it grows less.
Let my sword be my witness!—

div.p: [Who has come back and now stands behind Siegfried.

lg.l: So lightly I prize its worth.
I left it lying in a cavern,
Where a dragon once held watch.

div.p: Only this, not knowing its use.

lg.l: The gem of the Nibelung's art;
Its use, when worn on thy head,
Is to change thy shape as thou wilt;
If fain to be borne afar,
In a flash lo! thou art there!
Nay, Siegfried, let us not barter;
All I have a bauble poor,
Matched with thy treasure, would be.
I will serve thee without reward.

div.p: [Hagen has gone to Gutrune's door, and now opens it.
[Enters carrying a full drinking-horn, with which she approaches Siegfried.

lg.l: 'Tis his daughter gives thee to drink.

div.p: [Bows in a friendly manner and takes the horn, which he holds thoughtfully before him.
[He puts the drinking-horn to his lips and takes a long draught; then he hands it back to Gutrune, who, ashamed and confused, casts down her eyes. Siegfried gazes at her with sudden passion.

lg.l: Why sink them abashed by my gaze?
They kindle my blood; it flows

div.p: Gunther, what name is thy sister's?

lg.l: That in her eyes I am reading?
With thy brother I was fain to serve;
Were I to pray the same of thee,
Wouldst thou like him be proud?

div.p: [Gutrune involuntarily meets Hagen's eye. She bows her head humbly, and, expressing her feeling of unworthiness with a gesture, leaves the hall with faltering steps.
[Attentively watched by Hagen and Gunther, gazes after Gutrune as if entranced.

lg.l: My heart on one I have set
Whom there is no way to win.

div.p: He only who braves the fire...
[As if making an intense effort to remember something.
Siegfried hands the drinking-horn back to Gutrune, and gazes at her with sudden passion. See p. 119.
[Siegfried shows by a gesture that at the mention of Brünnhilde's name all remembrance of her has faded.

lg.l: I dare not essay the dread mountain;
The flames would not fall for me.

div.p: [Awakes from his dreamy state, and turns to Gunther high-spirited and gay.

lg.l: For thee I will win her,
Of fire I have no fear;
If Gutrun' I win as my wife.

div.p: Then let the oath now be sworn!

[Hagen fills a drinking-horn with fresh wine; he holds it out to Siegfried and Gunther, who cut their arms with their swords and hold them for a short pace over the horn; then they each lay two fingers on the horn, which Hagen continues to hold between them.

lg.l: Lo! I drop in the horn!
Bloom our blood in the draught!
Troth I drink to the friend

div.p: [Gunther drinks and hands the horn to Siegfried, who finishes the draught, and holds out the empty horn to Hagen. Hagen breaks the horn in two with his sword. Gunther and Siegfried join hands.
[Observes Hagen, who, while the oat was being sworn, has stood behind him.
Why hast not thou plighted thy troth?

lg.l: My blood had soured the good draught.

div.p: Heed not him and his spleen.
[He steps nearer to Gunther and points at him.

lg.l: And then bring home the bride.

div.p: [He turns to go, and beckons Gunther to follow him.
I am eager to be back.
[He goes to the shore to unmoor the boat.
Thou, Hagen, keep guard o'er the homestead.

[He follows Siegfried to the shore. Whilst Siegfried and Gunther, after laying their arms in the boat, are hoisting the sail and making ready for departure, Hagen takes up his spear and shield. Gutrune appears at the door of her chamber just as Siegfried is pushing off the boat, which immediately glides into the middle of the stream.
[While he seats himself comfortably with shield and spear in front of the hall.

lg.l: For wife seeking to win thee!

div.p: [She returns to her room greatly excited. Siegfried has seized an oar and rows the boat down-stream, so that it is soon lost to view.
[Sits motionless, his back against the door-post of the hall.

lg.l: Warding the hall from the foe:
And sails away for a wife;
And danger braves for his sake;
With her he brings me—the ring.
Gaily speed on in your pride!

div.p: [A curtain which frames the front of the hall is drawn, and cuts the stage off from the audience.

p.hi: The curtain is raised again. The rocky height as in the Prelude. Brünnhilde sits at the entrance to the cave in silent contemplation of Siegfried's ring. Moved by blissful memories, she covers the ring with kisses. Distant thunder is heard; she looks up and listens. She turns to the ring again. A flash of lightning. Again she listens, and looks into the distance, whence a dark thunder-cloud is approaching the rock.

lg.l: Who seeks the lonely one here?

div.p: Brünnhilde kisses the ring that Siegfried has left with her. See p. 124.
[Calling to the wing, and then hastening to the edge of the rock.

lg.l: And leave thy courser to rest.

div.p: [She runs into the wood, from which a loud sound like a thunder-clap is heard. She returns in great agitation with Waltraute, and remains joyfully excited without noticing the latter's anxious fear.

lg.l: And I know that his anger
Here to the rock I was bound,
Doomed to be thrall to the man
Who should wake the maid as he passed,
To bar to all cowards the road.
In light and laughter I live.

div.p: [She embraces Waltraute with wild manifestations of joy, which the latter tries with anxious impatience to repress.

lg.l: Hast thou been lured by my lot,
Far other the cause why I come,

div.p: [Here, for the first time, notices with surprise Waltraute's wildly excited state.

lg.l: So the stern one does not forgive?
At an end were my distress.
Mark with care what I say!
Drives me back to Walhall again.

div.p: What ails, then, the Gods everlasting?

lg.l: Give earnest heed to what I tell thee!
He wandered and roamed through the world.
A hero had cleft it asunder.
The logs as they hewed them,
High round the hall of the blest.
Who gathered in fear sit beside him.
The hall, ranged round in their order.
She would restore the ring that was theirs.
Both God and world were freed!'
And stormed in tumult to thee.
End thou the grief of the Gods!

div.p: The ravens of Wotan. See p. 128.
[She has thrown herself down before Brünnhilde.

lg.l: Sad one, are those thou dost tell?
I grasp not what thou art saying;
What wouldst thou, wild one, of me?

div.p: To the Rhine-daughters give it again.

lg.l: The accurst thing cast in the waves!
Ha! dost thou know what 'twould mean
Much is the fame of the Gods;
One glance at its shining gold,
One flash of its sacred fire
Than bliss of all the Gods
Shines from it bright and blessèd.
Ah, could I but utter the rapture
Repeat what I have told thee
That love I will not forswear,
Of love they never shall rob me;
Thus coldly thou leavest thy sister?
I will not part with the ring.

div.p: [She rushes away. A storm-cloud immediately rises from the wood, accompanied by thunder.
[As she looks after the brightly lit, retreating thunder-cloud, which soon vanishes in the distance.

lg.l: And may I see thee no more!

div.p: [Twilight has fallen. The light of the fire gradually shines more brightly from below. She gazes quietly out on the landscape.

lg.l: The flames that encircle me glow.

div.p: [The firelight approaches from below. Ever-brightening tongues of flame shoot up over the edge of the rock.

lg.l: The billows that blaze round the rock?

div.p: [Siegfried's horn is heard from the valley. Brünnhilde starts up in delight.

lg.l: With his horn greeting he sends!

div.p: [She hastens joyfully to the edge of the crag. Flames leap up, out of which Siegfried springs forward on to a high rock, whereupon the flames immediately withdraw and again only shine up from below. Brünnhilde recoils in terror, flies to the foreground, and from there, in speechless astonishment, stares at Siegfried, who, wearing the Tarnhelm, which covers the upper half of his face, leaving only his eyes free, appears in Gunther's form.
[Remaining on the rock at the back, motionless and leaning on his shield, regards Brünnhilde. In a feigned (harsher) voice.

lg.l: Whom thy fire did not dismay.
I want thee for my wife;
Thy pride by force at need.

div.p: [As before, beginning with a slightly tremulous voice, but continuing with more confidence.
[Springs down from the stone and approaches.
[Stretching out with a threatening gesture the finger on which she wears Siegfried's ring.

lg.l: Stand back! Fear thou this token!
While I am shielded by this,
Thou canst not force me to shame.
Wife it shall make thee to Gunther;
With this ring thou shalt be wed.
Nor dare, overbold, to draw near!

div.p: [He presses towards her. There is a struggle. Brünnhilde wrenches herself free, flies and turns round as if to defend herself. Siegfried seizes her again. She flies; he reaches her. They wrestle violently together. Siegfried catches her hand and draws the ring from her finger. She gives a loud scream. As she sinks helpless into his arms her unconscious look meets Siegfried's eyes. Siegfried lays her fainting on the stone bench at the entrance to the cave.

lg.l: Lead me the way to thy cave!

div.p: [Stares, as if fainting, before her; exhausted.
[Drives her on with a gesture of command. Trembling and with tottering steps she goes into the cave.

lg.l: And loyal been to my brother;
Lie betwixt me and his bride!

div.p: [He follows Brünnhilde. The curtain falls. In his natural voice.

div.head: THE SECOND ACT

p.hi: An open space on the shore in front of the Gibichungs' hall; to the right the open entrance to the hall, to the left the bank of the Rhine. From the latter, crossing the stage and mounting towards the back, rises a rocky height, cut by several mountain-paths. There an altar-stone to Fricka is visible, as well as one, higher up, to Wotan, and one at the side to Donner. It is night. Hagen, his arm round his spear and his shield by his side, fits against one of the pillars of the hall asleep. The moon shines out suddenly and throws a vivid light on Hagen and his immediate surroundings. Alberich is seen crouching in front of him, leaning his arms on Hagen's knees.

lg.l: And rest thou dost not hear?

div.p: [Softly, without moving, so that he seems to sleep on although his eyes are open.

lg.l: I hear thee, O baleful Niblung;
What wouldst thou tell me while I slumber?
As thy mother bore thee to me.
I have no cause to thank her
And he who captured my ring,
Through the Wälsung power and might.
He awaits in anguish his downfall.
He and all his must perish!
Sharest thou my hate and wrath.
When Fafner, the dragon, he slew.

div.p: The wooing of Grimhilde, the mother of Hagen. See p. 135

lg.l: Walhall and Nibelheim bow to his will.
By a wise woman is loved.
And no guile could win it again.
Like the Wälsung, Fafner in fight;
Putting Wälsung and Wotan to scorn!
Swear to me, Hagen, my son!

div.p: [From this point Alberich is covered by an ever-deepening shadow. At the same time day begins to dawn.

lg.l: The ring shall be mine yet;

div.p: Swear to me, Hagen, my son!
[Still gradually disappearing, and his voice, as he does so, becoming more and more inaudible.
[Alberich has quite disappeared. Hagen, who has never changed position, looks with fixed eyes and without moving towards the Rhine, over which the light of dawn is spreading.
"Swear to me, Hagen, my son!" See p. 138

p.hi: The gradually brightening red of dawn is reflected in the Rhine. Siegfried steps out suddenly from behind a bush close to the shore. He appears in his own shape, but has the Tarnhelm on his head still; he takes this off and, as he comes forward, hangs it on his girdle.

lg.l: 'Twas there that I drew the breath

div.p: [Gutrune comes from the hall to meet him.

lg.l: I come to thee with joyful news.
To the honour of all women!
For wife I have won thee to-day.

div.p: Comes then Brünnhild' with my brother?
None ever wooed with more ease.
Was he not scorched by the fire?

lg.l: It had not burnt him, I trow;
But I broke through it instead,
That I for wife might win thee.

div.p: And no harm didst thou take?
I laughed 'mid the surge of the flames.

lg.l: Like were we to a hair;

div.p: And so the bold maid was tamed?
Did she give herself to thee?
For her husband thou didst pass?

lg.l: Far as north from east and west,

div.p: But how got Gunther his wife from thee?

lg.l: Through the flames of the fire as they faded,
When day dawned, through the mist
She followed me down the hill;
A strong wind drives the lovers
Prepare to greet them with joy.

div.p: I can see a sail in the distance.

lg.l: Let us give her gracious greeting,
That glad and gay she here may tarry!
To the hall here for the wedding,
Our joy they will merrily share.

div.p: [As she goes towards the hall she turns round again.
[He gives her his hand and accompanies her into the hall.
[Has mounted a rock at the back, and starts blowing his cow-horn.
[Hagen remains where he is on the rock. Armed men arrive in haste by different paths; first singly, and then in larger and larger groups.

lg.l: And the foe put to flight?
How then can his vassals avail him?
And why hast callèd us here?

div.p: And after that, Hagen? Say, what next?

lg.l: That she may smile on the marriage!
When the beasts we have slain?
Drink, that the Gods, duly honoured,
Grace may accord to this marriage.

div.p: [Who has remained very grave, has come down to the men, and now stands among them.
[He points towards the Rhine. Some of the men hurry to the height; others range themselves on the shore to watch the arrival. Hagen goes up to some of the men.

[He turns slowly aside and moves towards the back. The boat arrives with Gunther and Brünnhilde. Those who have been looking out from the height come down to the shore. Some vassals spring into the water and pull the boat to land. All press closer to the bank.
[Gunther steps out of the boat with Brünnhilde.

lg.l: Health to thee and to thy bride!

div.p: [Presenting Brünnhilde, who follows him with pale face and lowered eyes, to the men.

lg.l: Here to the Rhine I bring.
The Gods have shown from of old

div.p: [Leads Brünnhilde, who never raises her eyes, to the hall, from which Siegfried and Gutrune, attended by women, now come forth. Gunther stops before the hall.

lg.l: By him who won thee for wife

div.p: [Brünnhilde, startled, looks up and sees Siegfried. Her eyes remain fixed on him in amazement. Gunther, who has released her violently trembling hand, shows, as do all present, blank astonishment at her behaviour.
[Goes a few steps towards Brünnhilde, who has begun to tremble.
[She sways and seems about to fall. Siegfried supports her.
[In Siegfried's arms, looking faintly up at him.
Gunther, see, thy wife is swooning!
[Perceives the ring on Siegfried's outstretched finger, and starts up with terrible vehemence.
[Mastering her terrible excitement, tries to control herself.
[Attentively regarding the ring on his finger.

lg.l: Thou who didst seize the ring
Make him yield up the pledge!
The ring? No ring I gave him,
Though thou dost know it well.
Where hast thou hid the ring
That thou didst capture from me?
Who despoiled me of the ring—

div.p: [All look expectantly at Siegfried, who seems to be lost in far-off thoughts as he contemplates the ring.

lg.l: When at Neidhöhl' boldly I fought,
And the mighty dragon was slain.
If it was by Gunther won,
And Siegfried has got it by guile.
For his guilt must the traitor pay.
The tongue that thus defames it
I must convict of its falsehood.
'Twixt me and this sad woman distraught
Full well I know its keenness,
When its lord won the woman he loved.

div.p: [The vassals form a ring round Siegfried and Hagen. Hagen holds out the spear; Siegfried lays two fingers of his right hand upon the point.

lg.l: Witness my oath sworn for ever!
When by death I am stricken
If what she tells is true,
And I broke faith with my friend!

div.p: [Strides furiously into the ring, tears Siegfried's hand from the spear, and grasps the point with her own.

lg.l: Witness my oath sworn for ever!
Be thy sharpness blessed by me,
For broken his oaths have been all,
And false is what he has sworn.
That the unbridled rage some demon
May have the chance to subside.
Ye vassals, go ye your ways;
Comes it to fighting with tongues.
Thou art not so vexed as I
But half have hid my face.
That I won her for thee
Thankful thy wife will be yet.
This day more merry than I!
Follow and share in my mirth!

div.p: [He throws his arm in the highest spirits round Gutrune and draws her into the hall. The vassals and women follow, carried away by his example. All go off, except Brünnhilde, Gunther, and Hagen. Gunther, in deep shame and dejection, with his face covered, has seated himself on one side. Brünnhilde, standing in the foreground, gazes for some time sorrowfully after Siegfried and Gutrune, then droops her head.

lg.l: I gave all my wisdom to him;
Will none of you lend a sword
With which I may sever my bonds?
Of his eye and its lightning—
Which streamed in its glory on me
Strength such as his to withstand!
How hard in battle to slay him;
For speeding him to his doom.
To preserve his body from harm.
And safely walks by spells enwound.

div.p: Then no weapon forged could wound him?

lg.l: Did the blow strike his back!
Or turn and fly, the foe pursuing,
So there I gave him no blessing.

div.p: And there shall my spear strike!
[He turns quickly from Brünnhilde to Gunther.

lg.l: Why hang thy head in grief?
No man has known such sorrow!
That breeds such cowards as thou!
Help, for my mother was thine—
And me ye all are betraying!
All the blood of the world
Would not atone for your guilt!

div.p: [Turning to Gunther and speaking to him secretly.

lg.l: If thou couldst capture the ring,
Which, alive, he never will yield.

div.p: His death would serve us all.

lg.l: How could we look in her face
If her husband we had slain?
That stole my husband's heart away!
If this grief we must give her,
We find him slain by a boar.
And mine I shall hold it!

div.p: [As Gunther turns impetuously towards the hall with Brünnhilde they are met by the bridal procession coming out. Boys and girls, waving flower-wreathed staves, leap merrily in front. The vassals are carrying Siegfried on a shield and Gutrune on a seat. On the rising ground at the back men-servants and maids are taking implements and beasts for sacrifice, by the various mountain-paths, to the altars, which they deck with flowers. Siegfried and the vassals blow wedding-calls on their horns. The women invite Brünnhilde to accompany them to Gutrune's side. Brünnhilde stares blankly at Gutrune, who beckons her with a friendly smile. As Brünnhilde is about to step back angrily Hagen comes quickly between them and presses her towards Gunther, who takes her hand again, whereupon he allows himself to be raised on a shield by the men. As the procession, scarcely interrupted, moves on quickly again towards the height, the curtain falls.

div.head: THE THIRD ACT

p.hi: A wild wooded and rocky valley on the Rhine, which flows past a steep cliff in the background. The three Rhine-Maidens, Woglinde, Wellgunde, and Flosshilde, rise to the surface and swim and circle as if dancing.

lg.l: Our father's gold shone on the billows.
How bright was once thy radiance,

div.p: [They sing and again start swimming and circling about. They pause and listen, then merrily splash the waters.

lg.l: Who again our gold shall give us!
Envy thine eye for its splendour.
Some elf has led me astray
And lured my feet from the path.

div.p: [Rise to the surface again and swim and circle as in a dance.
With what elf art thou so wroth?
Hast thou been tricked by some sprite?
Tell us, Siegfried; let us hear!

lg.l: So ask of me what you will.
I won the ring in fight;
And think ye for a worthless bear-skin
On you did I waste my goods,
My wife would have cause to scold.

div.p: Has the hero felt her hand?

lg.l: In grief ye shall be left,
Ye ask shall never be yours.

div.p: [The Rhine-Maidens have again joined hands for dancing.
How sad he should a miser be!

lg.l: The ring gladly I'd give them.
In grief ye shall be left,
Ye ask shall never be yours"
Come back; the ring shall be yours.

div.p: [He holds up the ring, which he has taken from his finger.
[Rise to the surface again. They appear grave and solemn.

lg.l: Until the harm thou hast felt
That in the ring lies hid.
Be freed by us from its curse.

div.p: [Calmly puts the ring on his finger again.

lg.l: Wilt thou not give to the Rhine
The ring to hide in its waters.
Was I firm when ye flattered,
I am firmer now when ye threaten!
Flee, oh, flee from the curse!
My sword once shattered a spear;
But he could not teach me to fear.
Has bestowed on me a ring.
And still for love might it be got,
But by threats to my life and my limbs—
The ring ye never shall gain.
Flee, oh, flee from the curse!"

div.p: [He lifts a clod of earth from the ground, holds it over his head, and with the last words throws it behind him.

lg.l: He is blind and in fetters bound fast.

div.p: [Wildly excited, they swim in wide circles close to the shore.

lg.l: And was false to his word;
And the ring that deals doom and death
Ere night falls thy wealth shall inherit.
Our cry by her will be heard.
To her! To her! To her!

div.p: [They turn quickly to their dance, and gradually swim away to the back singing.
[Looks after them smiling, one foot on a piece of rock and his chin resting on his hand.

lg.l: Still those who mistrust their smiles
They seek with threats to frighten,
At once they begin to scold.

div.p: [He looks calmly after the Rhine-Maidens, who have disappeared, and whose voices gradually die away. Horn-calls are then heard. Siegfried starts from a reverie and sounds his horn in answer.
[Having first answered the call with his horn.
[Appears on the height, followed by Gunther. He sees Siegfried.
Come down all! Here 'tis fresh and cool.
[The vassals now appear on the height, and come down with Hagen and Gunther.
[They lay the game in a heap.
[Wine-skins and drinking-horns are produced. All lie down.

lg.l: Now be the wonders told us
That chased the game from us.
No meal at all is mine;
To share with me your spoil.
A brood of three wild water-birds
I had caught and brought you.
Down there on the Rhine they told me
That slain to-day I should fall.

div.p: [Gunther starts and looks darkly at Hagen. Siegfried lies down between Gunther and Hagen.
[Whilst he orders a drinking-horn to be filled for Siegfried, and hands it to him.

lg.l: It has been rumoured, Siegfried, That thou canst tell the meaning

div.p: [He takes the drinking-horn and turns with it to Gunther, to whom he offers it after he has drunk from it.
Drink, Gunther, drink! Thy brother hands the draught!
[ Looks into the horn with horror. Moodily.
A pale draught thou hast poured!
With thine, then, be it mingled!
[He pours from Gunther's horn into his own so that it runs over.

lg.l: Thus mixed the wine flows over
May it prove a cordial kind!

div.p:
She speaks less plain to him
Than speak the birds to thee!

Since I have heard women singing.
The birds I have clean forgot.
But thou didst hear them once?

lg.l: If thou wouldst care to hear them.

div.p: [All lie down close to Siegfried, who alone sits upright.

lg.l: He might slay a dragon grim
That guarded treasure in the wood.
Out of the splinters of a weapon
The wood then we sought, and there
I have marvels to tell you.
And these I raised to my lips;
Was the blood by my tongue,
When what a bird was saying
On a bough it sat there and sang:
Tarnhelm, if he could but win it,
Would help him to deeds of renown;
And could he discover the ring,
It would make him the lord of the world!'

div.p: Was that the end of the singing?

lg.l: He sat above me and sang:—
Both the helm and the ring!
For Mime, too, covets the treasure,
He is bent on murdering Siegfried;
The steel that he forged not

div.p: [He has another drinking-horn filled, and drops the juice of a herb into it.
What further did the bird tell thee?

lg.l: It will mind thee of things long forgotten,
And bring old days to remembrance.

div.p: [He offers the horn to Siegfried, who looks into it thoughtfully and then drinks slowly.

lg.l: He sat there still and sang.
She sleeps where rugged rocks soar;
Ringed is her chamber by fire.
Till I came to the fire-ringed rock.
Sleeping, and clad in bright mail,
And waked the maid with my kiss.
Ah, then the burning, sweet embrace

div.p: [Two ravens fly up out of a bush, circle above Siegfried, and then fly away towards the Rhine.
[Siegfried starts up suddenly, and, turning his back to Hagen, looks after the ravens. Hagen thrusts his spear into Siegfried's back.

[Gunther and the vassals rush towards Hagen. Siegfried swings his shield on high with both hands in order to throw it on Hagen; his strength fails him; the shield drops from his grasp backwards, and he falls down upon it.
[Who have tried to hold Hagen back in vain.
[He turns calmly away, and is seen in the gathering twilight disappearing slowly over the height. Gunther bends over Siegfried in great grief. The vassals stand round the dying man full of sympathy.
[Supported by two vassals in a sitting posture, opens radiant eyes.

lg.l: And bound thee in slumber so fast?

div.p: [He sinks back and dies. The rest stand round him motionless and sorrowing. Night has fallen. At a silent command from Gunther the vassals raise Siegfried's body and bear it away slowly in a solemn procession over the height. The moon breaks through the clouds, and lights up the funeral procession with increasing clearness as it reaches the top of the hill. A mist has risen from the Rhine which gradually fills the whole stage, on which the funeral procession has become invisible. After a musical interlude the mist divides again, until at length the hall of the Gibichungs, as in Act I. appears with increasing distinctness.

p.hi: It is night. The moonlight is mirrored in the Rhine. Gutrune comes out of her chamber into the hall.

lg.l: I saw go down to the shore?

div.p: [She listens at the door at the right and calls.
[She opens the door timidly and looks into the inner room.

lg.l: I saw go downwards to the Rhine.

div.p: [Hagen's voice is heard outside coming nearer. When Gutrune hears it she stands for a time transfixed with terror.
[Increasing light from the torches is seen without. Hagen enters the hall.
[Men and women with lights and firebrands accompany, in great confusion, the procession returning with Siegfried's body.

lg.l: Or gaily go wooing fair women.

div.p: [The procession reaches the middle of the hall, and the vassals set down the body on a hastily improvised platform.

lg.l: 'Tis a wild boar's spoil they bring thee:

div.p: [Gutrune shrieks and falls upon the corpse. General emotion and mourning.

lg.l: These men have murdered my Siegfried!
Cast not the blame on me;
He is the accursèd wild boar
That did the hero to death.

div.p: With me art wroth for that?

lg.l: Yes, then, 'tis true that I slew him.
By my spear he falsely swore,
So by my spear he fell.
And what I claim is this ring.

div.p: Ye vassals, judge of my right!

lg.l: The Niblung son demands his own.

div.p: [He rushes on Gunther, who defends himself: they fight. The vassals throw themselves between. Gunther falls slain by a stroke from Hagen.
[He makes a grasp at Siegfried's hand, which raises itself in menace. All stand transfixed with horror.
[Advances firmly and solemnly from the background to the front. Still at the back.

lg.l: Now for vengeance his wife comes,
When milk is spilt by their mother;
Thou art the cause of our woe!
For, urged by thee, the men have slain him;
Cursèd hour that brought thee here!
Thou never wert wife of his;
But I am his lawful bride;
To me was the binding oath sworn,
Why didst thou give the poison
Whom through the draught he forgot.

div.p: [She turns from Siegfried in shame and fear, and, dying, bends over Gunther's body; remaining motionless in this position until the end. Hagen stands defiantly leaning on his spear and shield, sunk in gloomy thought, on the opposite side. Brünnhilde stands alone in the middle. After long and absorbed contemplation of Siegfried she turns with solemn exaltation to the men and women.

lg.l: And high by the Rhine be heaped;
Him who was first among men!
His horse lead to me here,
That with me his lord he may follow.
To have part in his glory
And share his honour in death.

div.p: [The young men, during the following, raise a great pyre of logs before the hall, near the bank of the Rhine; women decorate this with rugs, on which they strew plants and flowers.
[Absorbed anew in contemplation of Siegfried's dead face. Her expression brightens and softens as she proceeds.

lg.l: Barred he lay by his sword.
That else upon thee had fallen.
That wise a woman might grow!
Know I all thou wouldst learn?
By them I send thee back
Rest in peace now, O God!

div.p: [She signs to the vassals to bear Siegfried's body on to the pyre; at the same time she draws the ring off Siegfried's singer, and regards it musingly.

lg.l: For your counsel good, ye who dwell
In the waters deep of the Rhine.
The fire by which I am burnt
Cleanses the ring of its curse.
That stolen was to your grief!

div.p: [She has put the ring on her finger, and now turns to the pile of logs on which Siegfried's body lies stretched. Taking a great firebrand from one of the men, she waves it and points to the background.

lg.l: That ye have heard by the Rhine.

div.p: Brünnhilde on Grane leaps on to the funeral pyre of Siegfried—See p. 182

[She hurls the brand on to the pile of wood, which quickly breaks into flame. Two ravens fly up from the rock by the shore and vanish in the background. Brünnhilde perceives her horse, which has just been led in by two men.
[She springs towards him, and, catching hold of him, removes his bridle and bends towards him affectionately.

lg.l: To think thou shalt join him?
Have laid hold on my heart.

div.p: [She has swung herself on to the horse, and urges it forward.

lg.l: See! Brünnhild' greets thee, thy bride!

div.p: The Rhine-Maidens obtain possession of the ring and bear it off in triumph. See p. 182.

[She urges her horse with one leap into the burning pile of logs. The flames immediately blaze up, so that they fill the whole space in front of the hall and seem to catch hold of the building itself. The terrified men and women press as far to the front as possible. When the whole stage appears to be filled with fire the glow gradually fades, so that there is soon nothing left but a cloud of smoke, which drifts towards the back and hangs there as a dark bank of cloud. At the same time the Rhine overflows and the flood rolls up over the fire. The three Rhine-Maidens swim forward on the waves, and now appear over the spot where the fire was. Hagen, who since the incident of the ring has been watching Brünnhilde's behaviour with growing anxiety, is much alarmed by the fight of the Rhine-Maidens. He throws away his spear, shield, and helmet, and dashes into the flood as if mad, crying out, "Back from the ring!" Woglinde and Wellgunde fling their arms round his neck and, swimming away, draw him down with them into the depths. Flosshilde, swimming ahead of the others towards the back, joyously holds up the recovered ring. Through the bank of cloud on the horizon a red glow of increasing brightness breaks forth, and, illumined by this light, the Rhine-Maidens are seen merrily circling about and playing with the ring on the calmer waters of the Rhine, which has gradually retired to its natural bed. From the ruins of the fallen hall the men and women watch in great agitation the growing gleam of fire in the heavens. When this is at its brightest the hall of Walhall is seen, in which the Gods and heroes fit assembled, as described by Waltraute in the first Act. Bright flames seem to seize on the hall of the Gods. When the Gods are completely hidden by the flames the curtain falls.
